title: Out and about: shops, cafés and getting around
intro: Ask politely, order food, find your way and understand what people say back.

lessons.title: Polite requests
lessons.intro: In British English, polite words matter a lot. "Could I…?" sounds much better than "I want…".

phrases.en: Could I have a coffee, please?
phrases.note: The most useful request in English. Use it everywhere.

phrases.en: Can I get a receipt, please?
phrases.note: "Can I get" is common and fine in shops and cafés.

phrases.en: Would you mind helping me with this?
phrases.note: Very polite. After "Would you mind", use the -ing form.

phrases.en: Sorry, could you say that again?
phrases.note: Use this when you don't understand. People are happy to repeat.

phrases.en: Could you speak a bit more slowly, please?
phrases.note: Nobody will think this is strange.

phrases.en: Excuse me, do you work here?
phrases.note: "Excuse me" gets someone's attention. "Sorry" is for after you bump into someone.

phrases.en: That's all, thanks.
phrases.note: Say this when you've finished ordering or buying.

lessons.tip: Say "please" and "thank you" more than you think you need to. In the UK, "Thanks" or "Cheers" after almost every small service is normal.

lessons.title: At a café or restaurant
lessons.intro: From the table to the bill, these are the phrases you will hear and use.

phrases.en: A table for two, please.
phrases.note: Say the number of people.

phrases.en: Are you ready to order?
phrases.note: The waiter will ask this. Answer: "Yes, please" or "Could we have a few more minutes?"

phrases.en: I'll have the chicken curry, please.
phrases.note: "I'll have…" is the natural way to order food.

phrases.en: Is it spicy?
phrases.note: Ask about the food before you order.

phrases.en: Eat in or take away?
phrases.note: In cafés. Answer "Eat in, please" or "To take away".

phrases.en: Could we have the bill, please?
phrases.note: British: bill. American: check.

phrases.en: Can I pay by card?
phrases.note: Most places say "Yes, just tap it here" for contactless.

dialogue.line: Hi there, are you ready to order?
Yes, please. I'll have the chicken curry with rice.
Could I have a sparkling water, please?

lessons.title: Asking for directions
lessons.intro: Ask the way and understand the answer, including British words like "roundabout".

phrases.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
phrases.note: "How do I get to…?" works for any place.

phrases.en: Is it far from here?
phrases.note: The answer might be "It's about a ten-minute walk."

phrases.en: Go straight on, then take the second left.
phrases.note: "straight on" = keep going forward.

phrases.en: It's opposite the bank.
phrases.note: opposite = on the other side of the road, facing it.

phrases.en: It's next to the post office.
phrases.note: next to = beside.

phrases.en: Turn right at the roundabout.
phrases.note: A roundabout is a circle where roads meet. Very common in the UK.

phrases.en: Which bus goes to the city centre?
phrases.note: UK English: city centre. US: downtown.

lessons.tip: If someone gives long directions, repeat the main part back: "So, straight on and second left?" It checks you understood and gives them a chance to correct you.

cards.meaning: A piece of paper that shows what you paid. The p is silent: "ri-SEET".
cards.example: Do you want the receipt in the bag?

cards.meaning: A line of people waiting; to wait in a line.
cards.example: There was a long queue at the post office.

cards.meaning: The money you get back when you pay too much.
cards.example: Here's your change, 50p.

cards.meaning: Paying by touching your card or phone on the machine.
cards.example: Can I pay contactless?

cards.meaning: Money given back when you return something.
cards.example: I'd like a refund for these shoes.

cards.meaning: Cheaper than usual for a short time.
cards.example: Rice is on offer this week: buy one, get one free.

cards.meaning: The paper that shows how much you must pay in a restaurant.
cards.example: Could we have the bill, please?

cards.meaning: Food you buy and eat somewhere else. Also "a takeaway".
cards.example: Shall we get a takeaway tonight?

cards.meaning: A small dish you eat before the main course.
cards.example: We shared a starter and then had pizza.

cards.meaning: To reserve a table, ticket or appointment.
cards.example: I booked a table for eight o'clock.

cards.meaning: On the other side, facing something.
cards.example: The bank is opposite the station.

cards.meaning: A circular junction where several roads meet.
cards.example: Take the third exit at the roundabout.

cards.meaning: British: the path for walking beside a road. US: sidewalk.
cards.example: Please walk on the pavement.

cards.meaning: A ticket to go somewhere and come back.
cards.example: A return ticket to Manchester, please.

cards.meaning: A ticket for one direction only.
cards.example: Just a single to Leeds, please.

cards.meaning: Where you wait to get on a train.
cards.example: The train leaves from platform 4.

cards.meaning: Later than planned.
cards.example: The 8:15 train is delayed by ten minutes.

cards.meaning: A very polite way to ask someone to do something. Use -ing after it.
cards.example: Would you mind opening the window?

cards.meaning: British: nice, good. Often used by shop staff to mean "OK, great".
cards.example: Lovely, that's £4.50 please.

cards.meaning: To add more money to a card or phone.
cards.example: I need to top up my bus card.

quiz.q: Which is the most polite way to order?
options: Could I have a coffee, please?
quiz.explain: "Could I have…, please?" is polite and natural.
After "Would you mind", use the -ing form: closing.

quiz.q: In a British restaurant, you ask for the ___.
quiz.explain: British English: the bill. American English: the check.

quiz.q: "The bank is opposite the station" means the bank is…
options: on the other side of the road from the station
quiz.explain: Opposite = facing it, on the other side.

quiz.q: You want to travel to London and come back. You buy a…
quiz.explain: A return ticket is there and back. A single is one way.

quiz.q: You didn't understand. What do you say?
options: Sorry, could you say that again?
quiz.explain: "Sorry, could you say that again?" is polite and very common.

quiz.q: Rice is "on offer". This means it is…
quiz.explain: On offer = on special sale for a short time.

speak.text: Could I have a coffee, please?
Sorry, could you say that again a bit more slowly?
I'll have the chicken curry with rice, please.
Could we have the bill, please? Can I pay by card?
Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
Go straight on, then turn right at the roundabout.
A return ticket to Manchester, please.
Would you mind helping me with these bags?

questions.q: Hi there! What can I get you today?
tips: Order one drink and one thing to eat.
Answer the question "Eat in or take away?"
questions.model: Hi, could I have a large latte and a chicken sandwich, please? To take away, please. Can I pay contactless?

questions.q: You bought a jacket, but it's too small. What do you say to the shop assistant?
tips: Say what you want: a different size or a refund.
Mention that you have the receipt.
questions.model: Hi, I bought this jacket here last week, but it's too small for me. Could I change it for a bigger size? If you don't have one, I'd like a refund, please. I've got the receipt here.

questions.q: Someone asks you: "Excuse me, is there a supermarket near here?" Give them directions.
tips: Say if it's near or far.
Use: go straight on, turn left/right, it's next to / opposite…
questions.model: Yes, there's one about five minutes from here. Go straight on down this road, then take the first left. The supermarket is on your right, opposite the bank.
